Javan rusa fawns are born after a gestation period that researchers have carefully documented under controlled thermal conditions. At the typical core body temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C] observed in this tropical cervid, the gestation interval averages 251 days [tg = 251 days], with most births falling within a narrow range of 249 to 253 days. Neonates weigh approximately 4000 grams [Wwb = approximately 4000 grams], though field surveys indicate a broader spectrum of 3 to 5 kilograms at delivery. This birth mass is modest relative to the adult dimensions the calf will ultimately achieve, a pattern consistent with other members of the genus Rusa. The newborn fawn, a precocial neonate, is capable of standing within hours of parturition, a critical adaptation for evading predators in the dense monsoon forests and grasslands of Java and Timor. Maternal investment during gestation is substantial, given the relatively long developmental period in utero, and the birth event itself represents the culmination of nearly nine months of embryogenesis and foetal growth under tightly regulated physiological conditions.

Weaning represents a significant nutritional transition for the developing young, marking the cessation of lactation and the onset of complete dietary independence from the dam. Under production conditions, Javan rusa calves are typically weaned at 92 days following birth [tx = 92 days following birth], a value that corresponds to approximately three months of age at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. At this developmental stage, the weanling has attained a wet weight of approximately 20,400 grams [Wwx = approximately 20,400 grams], reflecting the rapid somatic growth sustained by the high-quality milk characteristic of tropical deer species. This weight gain trajectory from the 4000 gram [Wwb = 4000 gram] birth mass involves a more than fivefold increase in body size over a relatively short suckling period. Such rapid mass accumulation, driven by the high lipid content of maternal milk, is comparable to growth rates observed in other tropical cervids and underscores the energetic efficiency of the mother-offspring dyad during the pre-weaning phase. The dietary transition itself involves a gradual shift from exclusive milk ingestion to the consumption of solid forage, a process that typically begins several weeks before complete nutritional emancipation. In wild populations, the timing of weaning may be influenced by seasonal resource availability, though the 92-day benchmark derived from managed herds provides a reliable reference for the species.

Puberty in Javan rusa is attained at different ages depending on environmental conditions and management practices, with two distinct developmental schedules reported in the literature. Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of healthy, well-nourished individuals maintaining a core temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C], some females achieve sexual maturity as early as 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth], which corresponds to approximately one year of age. This relatively rapid pubertal onset is characteristic of small-bodied females that have experienced accelerated growth. However, a more commonly observed schedule places the attainment of gonadal maturation at 730 days after birth [tp = 730 days after birth], or roughly two years of age, particularly in males and in individuals from less productive habitats at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This later maturation reflects the energetic demands of achieving the necessary body condition and fat reserves required to support reproductive function, and aligns with the delayed reproductive schedules seen across many polygynous cervids. The variability in pubertal timing highlights the species' adaptive capacity to adjust life-history schedules in response to nutritional and thermal regimes.

Adult body size in Rusa timorensis exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, a trait common among polygynous ungulates. Females attain an ultimate wet weight of 91,000 grams [Wwi = 91,000 grams] once fully grown, a value that represents the asymptotic mass achieved during their adult life. Males, by contrast, reach a substantially larger ultimate wet weight of 96,500 grams [Wwi = 96,500 grams], reflecting both their larger skeletal frame and the greater muscle mass associated with intrasexual competition during the rut. This difference of roughly five to six percent in total body mass is accompanied by marked differences in antler development, with males carrying large, branched antlers that are shed and regrown annually. Both sexes continue to add body mass gradually after reaching reproductive maturity, though the most rapid phase of somatic growth occurs during the juvenile and sub-adult stages. Reported values for maximum adult body mass suggest that individuals from the larger island populations, particularly those on Timor, may occasionally exceed the typical female and male benchmarks under exceptionally favourable forage conditions.

The lifespan of Javan rusa in natural settings has been estimated from long-term field studies, with data collected under the typical core temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C] yielding a maximum longevity of approximately 21.1 years [am = approximately 21.1 years]. Annual reproductive output is modest, with females producing a single offspring per parturition event [N_R_i = single offspring per parturition event] and typically achieving a maximum of one reproductive event per year [F_R_i = one reproductive event per year], reflecting the constraints imposed by the lengthy 251-day (251 days) [tg = 251 days] gestation period and extended lactation at a temperature of 38.6 °C [T = 38.6 °C]. This low intrinsic fecundity, typical of long-lived deer species with high maternal investment, is offset by substantial per-offspring provisioning, as evidenced by the large weaning mass relative to birth mass. Population growth under favourable conditions is therefore gradual, with recruitment heavily dependent on adult survival rather than high reproductive turnover.
